personalEssay.prompt: Describe a role you play that others might overlook.
personalEssay.text:
The calling script for our spring production of Our Town had 214 cues in it. I know because I numbered every one in pencil, and then numbered them again when the director cut a scene a week before opening. As stage manager for Lakeshore Regional Theatre Company, I sit in the booth with a headset and a prompt book and say "Go" more times in a night than most people say it in a year.

I started stage managing in tenth grade, when the senior who had the job graduated and nobody else wanted it. I thought it would be clerical. It turned out to be the opposite: a stage manager's job is to know where everyone is and what they need before they ask. We do three shows a year, and I run a crew of twelve, most of whom are louder than I am. I learned to be calm on headset because panic travels down a wire faster than anything.

The same skill turned out to matter at home. Last year my grandmother had a stroke, and since then I have spent Tuesday and Thursday evenings at her apartment. I cook dinner, sort her pills into the plastic days-of-the-week box, and drive her to physical therapy. She used to be a seamstress, and she still critiques my costume crew's hems from photos on my phone. Caring for her has its own calling script: medications at six, dinner at six-thirty, the evening news at seven, which she argues with.

On Saturdays I am at Northshore Bread Company by five in the morning. The ovens are already hot when I arrive, and I shape loaves until the doors open at seven. This summer the owner gave me a key and started letting me open alone. I don't think I have ever felt so trusted by a piece of metal.

One summer I also apprenticed in lighting design with the Duluth Playhouse summer youth program, where I hung and focused sixty fixtures for two musicals. Climbing a ladder with a wrench clipped to my belt taught me that every soft pool of light on stage is the result of someone sweating on a catwalk. It made me a better stage manager, because now I know what I am asking for when I call a cue.

At the Minnesota Thespian Festival last year, I presented my prompt book from Our Town and received a Superior rating in stage management. The judge asked why I had numbered my cues twice. I told her the truth: because plans change, and the people depending on you should never be the ones who pay for it.

I want to study theater, and maybe arts management, because I like making space for other people to be brilliant. The booth is dark and nobody claps for it. That is fine. I know the show could not happen without someone saying "Go."

supplements.prompt: What would you contribute to the Northwestern community?
supplements.text:
I would bring a prompt book. Not literally, though I will probably pack one. I mean the habit behind it: writing down what everyone needs before they need it.

Since tenth grade I have been the stage manager at Lakeshore Regional, running a twelve-person crew through three productions a year. I am the one who knows that the actor playing Emily needs water stage left after Act Two, and that the fly rail sticks when the building is cold. At home, I keep a different kind of prompt book for my grandmother, whom I care for two evenings a week: medications, appointments, the name of her physical therapist's dog.

At Northwestern, I want to study theater and learn from student-run groups where undergraduates design, direct, and manage their own shows. I would love to stage-manage for a student company in my first year and learn from people who are better at this than I am.

I would also bring a key-holder's sense of responsibility. Every Saturday at five in the morning I unlock a bakery because someone trusts me to. I would like to earn that kind of trust again.
